pages.title: Title
pages.summary: Momentum.

pages.title: Roadmap
pages.summary: JT 1993 (the effect, profit decomposition), MG 1999 (industries), the explanation debate + out-of-sample, DM 2013/2016 (crashes, dynamic strategy), refinements & disposition effect. ~12%/yr spread the CAPM and FF3 can't explain.

pages.title: What momentum is
pages.summary: 6–12-month relative winners keep winning; buy winners/short losers (zero-investment). JT 1963–90: ~12%/yr abnormal. Violates even weak-form efficiency; beta-neutral; the FF3 model's biggest puzzle.

pages.title: Horizon regimes
pages.summary: Reversal <1mo (Jegadeesh 1990, Lehmann 1990); momentum 3–12mo (JT); reversal 3–5yr (DeBondt–Thaler). Annual Sharpe by lookback: 1mo −0.82; 3mo 0.18; 6mo 0.46; 12mo 0.58; 24mo 0.10; 36mo −0.42; 60mo −0.58. Profits dissipate after a year, reverse after 2–3 ⟹ temporary price effect.

pages.title: The simple strategy + deciles
pages.summary: Rank on past 6–12mo, decile portfolios, overlapping 6/6 windows (1/6 turnover/mo). 1965–2008 monthly returns: P1 0.46, P2 0.09, P3 1.05, P4 1.12, P5 1.15, P6 1.18, P7 1.21, P8 1.30, P9 1.41, P10 1.63; 10−1 = 1.17%/mo (~14% annualized).

pages.title: Decomposition: algebra
pages.summary: π from weights w=(r_{t−1}−r̄): E[(r_j−r̄)(r_{j,t−1}−r̄_{t−1})] = (μj−μ̄)² + (βj−β̄)²Cov(F,F₋₁) + Cov(εt,ε_{t−1}).

pages.title: Three candidate sources
pages.summary: E[π] = σμ² + σβ²·Cov(F,F₋₁) + avg own-autocovariance. Factor-timing term is WRONG-SIGNED (market autocovariance <0) ⟹ profits come from positive firm-specific autocovariance: delayed reaction to firm news (JT).

pages.title: Underreaction or lead–lag?
pages.summary: Alternative: delayed reaction to COMMON shocks (β₂F_{t−1}). JT: skipping a week should mute lead-lag, yet profits GROW. Puzzle: firm-specific shocks are diversifiable — why isn't this arbitraged away?

pages.title: Omega decomposition
pages.summary: E[π] = tr(Ω)/N − 1'Ω1/N² + σμ² = own-autocov − cross-serial cov + mean dispersion. The three terms ARE the three explanations: underreaction (JT), lead-lag, Conrad–Kaul (no predictability needed).

pages.title: MG: industry split
pages.summary: ε = δ_industry + ε*. Which covariance survives? μ-persistence: no. Factor/beta momentum: wrong sign. Industry autocovariance: the live channel. Disputes: Grundy–Martin (both positive), Conrad–Kaul (σμ², rejected by both).

pages.title: MG Table 1
pages.summary: (6,6) WML monthly: raw 0.0043 (t 4.65); size&B/M-adj 0.0029 (3.34); raw−industry 0.0013 (2.04); size,B/M&industry-adj 0.0008 (0.91) — collapses. Industry momentum 0.0043 (4.24); random industries −0.0005 (−1.09).

pages.title: Cross-section 1927–2009
pages.summary: Quintiles: avg returns 6.0/9.7/11.0/13.6/18.0%/yr; beta-adjusted excess −4.5/1.1/3.2/5.8/9.1. Spread ~12%/yr raw, 13.6 adjusted; losers earn NEGATIVE risk-adjusted returns.

pages.title: FF regressions 1927–2012
pages.summary: Decile alphas: P1 −0.67 (t −3.43) … P10 +0.87 (t 8.00); WML alpha 1.53%/mo (t 5.93). Losers load positive on SMB (0.51) and HML (0.38) — small distressed value-like; winners growth-like (h −0.29); WML s=−0.25, h=−0.68: the factors push the WRONG way, alpha grows. R² up to 0.94: factors price variation, not means.

pages.title: The fourth factor
pages.summary: Carhart: MKT+SMB+HML+UMD (12−1 skip most recent month). Factor models explain 80–90% of variation, not the mean; alpha stable across a century; risk adjustment improves profits (Grundy–Martin 2001).

pages.title: Explanation 1: risk
pages.summary: Problems: risers are LESS risky; factor momentum wrong-signed; Sharpe too high. Bad states: bear markets mkt −4.43 vs WML +1.46; recessions −1.59 vs +0.89 — momentum pays in bad states, opposite of a risk premium.

pages.title: Explanation 2: behavioral
pages.summary: Gradual info diffusion + reference points (DHS 1998, BSV 1998, Hong–Stein 1999; disposition, tax-loss). Problem: looks like near-arbitrage — needs limits to arbitrage. Tension: momentum = short-horizon UNDERreaction; value = long-horizon OVERreaction.

pages.title: Explanation 3: data mining — over time
pages.summary: VW WML: 1927–2012 mean 0.75 (t 4.85); pre-sample 1927–64: 0.64 (2.60); original 1965–89: 0.83 (4.03); post-publication 1990–2012: 0.93 (2.85), 3F alpha 1.17 (3.27) — biggest AFTER fame.

pages.title: Across markets & assets (AMP)
pages.summary: Sharpe 1972–2010 (15% vol scale): US .45, UK .47, Europe .76, Japan .12, global stocks .68; equity indices .63, currencies .32, bonds .17, commodities .51; EW other .65; EW ALL 0.81 (12.1%/yr). Positive everywhere.

pages.title: Where momentum is strongest
pages.summary: Stronger where news diffuses slowly: small, low-analyst-coverage (HLS 1999 — concentrated in LOSERS: bad news travels slowly), high-volume (Lee–Swaminathan), growth (Asness 1997); robustness Israel–Moskowitz 2013.

pages.title: Coverage/size/volume chart
pages.summary: Fraction of profits from winners vs losers within coverage/size/volume terciles.

pages.title: The risk of momentum
pages.summary: 2000–03 poor; spring 2009 disaster. Industry concentration = less diversified, tracking error. Are Sharpes even right given the fat left tail?

pages.title: Monthly WML series
pages.summary: 1927–2011: worst months −45 to −50%, clustered 1930s and 2009.

pages.title: Left-skewed distribution
pages.summary: WML monthly histogram: mean 9.0%, sd 16.2%, Sharpe 0.6, skew −3.0, kurtosis 28.7 — small steady gains, rare huge losses.

pages.title: Crashes: the phenomenon
pages.summary: Skew −6.3 monthly (HML +1.8, market −0.58); max month +26.1%; five worst −79/−60/−46/−44/−42%; Apr 2009 worst since Aug 1932. Like being short an OTM put (BNP 2008). Plan: characterize → time-varying betas → hedge → ~double the Sharpe.

pages.title: The 2009–10 crash
pages.summary: Past losers gained ≈487% off the March 2009 bottom; momentum left behind.

pages.title: Great Depression replay
pages.summary: 1932–45: market →$26.63, losers →$6.2, winners →$3.7.

pages.title: Cumulative log WML
pages.summary: Decades of compounding punctured by 1932 and 2009.

pages.title: Portfolio characteristics
pages.summary: WML 1927–2010: mean 14.4%, Sharpe 0.52, market beta −0.54, alpha 18.4% (t 6.5), monthly skew −6.32 (daily −1.47).

pages.title: Ten worst months
pages.summary: All but one (Jan 2001) follow a deeply NEGATIVE 2-yr market, and the contemporaneous month is POSITIVE every time — crashes are bear-market rebounds.

pages.title: Turning points
pages.summary: Jul–Aug 1932: market +82%, losers +236% vs winners +30% (−206 pts). Mar–May 2009: market +29%, losers +156% vs winners +6.5% (−149 pts).

pages.title: Losers as OTM options
pages.summary: 2009 losers (Citi, BofA, Ford, GM) down 90%+, levered, near-bankrupt — equity = OTM call on firm value (Merton 1974) ⟹ huge up-market betas; winners defensive. State-dependent beta gap is the proximate crash cause.

pages.title: Conditional betas
pages.summary: Rolling: loser beta ≈2.5 (1930s), ≈3.7 (2009); winner ≈1 ⟹ WML beta deeply negative in rebounds.

pages.title: Hedging (Grundy–Martin)
pages.summary: Rolling 42-day betas with 10 market lags; hedged r_WML − βt·r_m. Removing the market component should cut the tail without losing alpha.

pages.title: Hedged vs unhedged 1928–45
pages.summary: Unhedged collapses in 1932; hedged compounds — the crash was beta risk.

pages.title: Up/down-beta regression
pages.summary: Normal WML beta ≈0.05; bear markets −0.79 more; a further −0.70 when the bear-market month is UP. Down-then-up = the crash state.

pages.title: Dynamic strategies
pages.summary: Constant-vol (Barroso–Santa-Clara): scale by σtgt/σ̂. Dynamic (DM): w ∝ (1/2λ)·μ̂/σ̂². Sharpes 1927–2011: WML 0.52, const-σ 0.87, dynamic 1.12; by sub-period dynamic wins everywhere (2000–11: 0.02→0.63).

pages.title: Cumulative comparison
pages.summary: Dynamic dominates by avoiding 1932 and 2009.

pages.title: International replication (JFE Table 9)
pages.summary: Europe α 8.9%/yr, bear Δβ −0.51, optionality −0.42; Japan/UK/global similar — written-call behavior in every market; ex-ante variance predicts low momentum returns everywhere.

pages.title: Other asset classes (Table 10)
pages.summary: Commodities bear Δβ −0.73, optionality −1.10 (sig); currencies −1.09; all-assets −0.37/−0.61. Problem for Merton: futures and currencies aren't levered equity, yet crash the same way.

pages.title: Dynamic everywhere (Table 11)
pages.summary: Sharpe WML→const-σ→dynamic: US .28→.52→.65; Europe .46→.89→1.13; Japan .07→.16→.42 (resurrected); all assets .75→.94→1.14; fully dynamic 1.22. Skew flips positive; dynamic spans const-σ.

pages.title: DM conclusions
pages.summary: Normal times: underreaction. Extremes: loser rallies = crashes tied to past market losses and lagged vol. Beta risk doesn't explain the premium but hedging it doubles the Sharpe. Replicates across 8 markets/asset classes.

pages.title: A family of underreaction
pages.summary: PEAD and dividend drift; earnings momentum (analyst revisions; distinct from price momentum; combined is better; 34 markets); disposition effect (Grinblatt–Han 2005, Frazzini 2006). Across securities: volume, stocks→bonds, industry→suppliers, customers→suppliers.

pages.title: PEAD & earnings momentum charts
pages.summary: CAR by SUE quintile drifts for ~60 days; revision quintiles drift ~12 months (Bernard–Thomas 1989; Chan–Jegadeesh–Lakonishok 1996).

pages.title: Disposition & overhang
pages.summary: Sell winners too early, ride losers (mental accounting + prospect theory) ⟹ prices underreact. Frazzini: overhang g=(P−RP)/P from fund holdings; drift worst when news and overhang share sign.

pages.title: Prospect-theory figures
pages.summary: Risk-seeking over losses (hold), risk-averse over gains (sell).

pages.title: Frazzini event drift
pages.summary: Price paths around news by overhang sign.

pages.title: Frazzini alphas
pages.summary: Aligned news+overhang: L/S drift ~2.1–2.5%/mo; conflicting: vanishes.

pages.title: Frazzini robustness
pages.summary: Survives ownership, turnover, characteristics, SUE, revisions.

pages.title: Trade imbalances (Lee–Ready)
pages.summary: Sign trades vs bid-ask midpoint; small vs large trades = individuals vs institutions. Hvidkjaer: small-trade imbalances drive momentum; large traders show no underreaction.

pages.title: Imbalance figures
pages.summary: Winners: initial small-trade buying converts to selling over the next year — underreaction then delayed reaction by individuals.

pages.title: Cohen–Frazzini: Callaway/Coastcast
pages.summary: Callaway = 50% of Coastcast sales; July 2001 guidance cut −30%; Coastcast barely moved, then drifted down for weeks.

pages.title: Customer momentum table
pages.summary: Sort suppliers on customers' last-month return: L/S xret 1.58 (t 3.8); 3F alpha 1.56 (3.6); 4F alpha 1.38 (3.1) ≈18%/yr. Limited attention to public links.

pages.title: Customer-driven drift figure
pages.summary: +3.9% in the customer-return month, +4.7% further drift over ~12 months.

pages.title: Conclusions
pages.summary: Large, monotone, out-of-sample robust; the fourth factor; much is industry momentum; danger = conditional crash risk. Open: real or fleeting, risk or behavior, arbitrage erosion. Investor job: size to survive crashes; hedge/scale the time-varying betas.
